big: Two bonds, same five years. One pays 7%, the other 9.5%. Which would you take? Most people say the second. The better question is: why does it pay more?

lines: A company bond is offering 11% while the government pays 7%. Why would I take 7%?
A good question to ask. A higher rate usually comes with a reason. Let us look at who is on the other side of the loan.

alt: Two sets of bars comparing a government bond and a company bond on interest and on safety
caps: The government offers a lower rate.
The company offers more, but it is also more likely to run into trouble.
The safety scores are made up to show the trade-off, not real ratings.
The extra interest is the price of taking on more credit risk.

title: Is a high rate good news?
stops: A higher rate often means higher credit risk
A credit rating is a guarantee of repayment
Government bonds carry the lowest default risk
All company bonds are equally safe
alt: A shield checking four statements about bond safety
caps: Extra interest is usually paid for extra risk.
A rating is an opinion on repayment, not a promise.
Government bonds sit at the safe end of rupee bonds.
Companies differ a lot. Read the rating before you buy.

q: A company bond pays 11% while a government bond pays 7%. What does the extra 4% most likely signal?
opts: The company is certain to repay, so the lender gets a bonus for patience
The government is hiding losses, so its rate is artificially low in the market
Lenders are paid extra for the higher chance that the company may not repay
Nothing at all, since bond rates are set at random for each new issue
why: Extra interest does not signal certainty. It more often points to higher doubt about repayment.
Government rates are low because default risk is low, not because of any hidden losses.
A higher rate usually compensates for credit risk, so the extra is the price of that doubt.
Rates are not random. They reflect the borrower's risk, the term and market conditions.

q: A bond carries a top credit rating from a rating agency. What does the rating tell you?
opts: The agency sees low default risk, but it is an opinion, not a guarantee
The bond is insured by the government up to ₹5 lakh per investor
The borrower can never miss a payment, so the bond has no risk left
The bond's price will not move, since top ratings fix the price for good
why: A rating is the agency's view of repayment ability. It can be wrong and can change over time.
Deposit insurance applies to bank deposits. It does not cover bonds, whatever their rating.
Even top-rated borrowers can run into trouble. A rating lowers the chance, not to zero.
Prices of bonds, even top-rated ones, move with interest rates. Ratings do not fix prices.

q: A company misses its scheduled interest payment on a bond. What has happened, and what does it mean for lenders?
opts: A routine delay that the bond rules always allow for each year
A maturity, so lenders receive their principal back early
A rating upgrade, since the company is saving cash for growth
A default, so lenders may have to wait longer or accept a loss
why: A missed payment is not routine. Bond terms set fixed dates, and missing one is a serious event.
Maturity is a planned end date. It is not the same as missing a payment.
A missed payment is a warning sign. It leads to downgrades, not upgrades.
Missing a due payment is a default, and lenders may be paid late, partly, or not at all.

q: For the same time period, which borrower's bond would normally pay the lowest interest rate?
opts: A new company with no track record, because it is easiest to start
The Government of India, since it carries the lowest default risk
A mid-sized company with a good rating, since it is well known
A bank's subsidiary that has just been formed this year
why: A new company is riskier, so it must pay more to attract lenders, not less.
Lending to the government is treated as the safest rupee loan, so it pays the least extra.
A good rating still carries more risk than the government, so the rate would be higher.
A newly formed firm has no history to judge, so lenders would expect a higher rate.

pts: A higher rate usually means higher credit risk.
A credit rating is an opinion on repayment, not a guarantee.
Government bonds carry the lowest default risk among rupee bonds.
